title: Iodine Deficiency
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis; deficiency leads to congenital hypothyroidism, cretinism and goiter. In low‑resource settings, diet, soil, and infections worsen the problem.

sections.p: Iodine is a trace element incorporated into thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). The thyroid gland concentrates iodine from plasma via the sodium‑iodide symporter (NIS).
b: Iodine is absorbed in the duodenum; 80–90% is taken up by the thyroid.
Urinary iodine excretion reflects recent intake; <100 µg/L indicates deficiency.

t.b: Measures recent iodine intake; <100 µg/L = deficiency, 100–199 µg/L = borderline, ≥200 µg/L = adequate.

sections.p: Iodide is oxidised by thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and organified onto tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin, forming monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT). Coupling yields T3 and T4.
b: T4 is secreted in larger amounts; T3 is the active hormone.
T4 is converted to T3 in peripheral tissues by deiodinases.

t.b: Elevated when thyroid hormone production is low; indicates primary hypothyroidism.
Low in hypothyroidism; normal in subclinical.

sections.p: TSH from the pituitary stimulates iodine uptake and hormone synthesis. Negative feedback by T4/T3 suppresses TSH.
b: TSH rises when T4 falls; TSH is the most sensitive screen for hypothyroidism.

t.b: Primary hypothyroidism: TSH >4.5 mIU/L with low free T4.

sections.p: Iodine deficiency impairs hormone synthesis, leading to low T4/T3, high TSH, and compensatory goiter. In pregnancy, fetal brain development is halted, causing cretinism.
b: Congenital hypothyroidism: severe mental retardation, growth failure, umbilical hernia.
Acquired hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation.

t.b: Detects congenital hypothyroidism; a TSH >20 mIU/L warrants referral.

sections.p: In East Africa, high‑altitude, soil erosion, and reliance on unfortified salt increase risk. HIV, malaria, and malnutrition can mask or worsen symptoms.
b: Goiter is the most common visible sign; patients may present with growth delay or developmental lag.

t.b: Shows diffuse enlargement; nodules uncommon in pure iodine deficiency.

sections.p: When laboratory access is limited, a pragmatic approach uses clinical signs, urinary iodine, and TSH.
b: If TSH >10 mIU/L and free T4 low, treat as hypothyroidism.

t.b: Shows recent intake; <100 µg/L confirms deficiency.
High indicates primary hypothyroidism; normal TSH with low free T4 suggests central.
Differentiates diffuse goiter from nodular disease.

sections.p: Treat the underlying deficiency and support thyroid function.
b: Iodine supplementation: iodised salt or potassium iodide tablets.
Levothyroxine replacement if TSH >10 mIU/L or symptomatic.
Monitor TSH every 6–12 months; adjust dose to keep TSH 0.5–2.5 mIU/L.

t.b: Prevents goiter and congenital hypothyroidism; avoid excess to prevent hyperthyroidism.
Chosen for its safety profile; avoid amiodarone or lithium in endemic areas due to iodine load.

sections.p: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, iodine‑induced hyperthyroidism, and subclinical hypothyroidism.
b: Hashimoto’s: anti‑TPO antibodies positive; nodules may be present.
Iodine‑induced hyperthyroidism: sudden rise in iodine intake causes thyrotoxicosis.

t.b: Positive in autoimmune disease; negative in pure iodine deficiency.

sections.p: Urinary iodine can be falsely low in chronic renal failure; TSH may be normal in early deficiency.
b: In pregnancy, TSH reference ranges shift; use trimester‑specific values.

t.b: Lower in first trimester; use 0.1–4.0 mIU/L for screening.

sections.p: Remember the 200 µg/L urinary iodine cut‑off for adequacy. In a resource‑poor setting, a high TSH with low free T4 is diagnostic. Avoid iodine loading in patients with known thyroid disease.
b: Use iodised salt as first‑line public health measure.

t.b: Confirms deficiency; counsel on diet and salt iodisation.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe mental retardation in infancy, persistent goiter with compressive symptoms, unexplained weight gain with cold intolerance, or sudden onset of hyperthyroid symptoms after iodine supplementation.

faq.a: Yes, excessive iodine intake can trigger the Wolff‑Chaikoff effect reversal, leading to thyrotoxicosis, especially in those with pre‑existing thyroid disease.

faq.q: What foods are good iodine sources in East Africa?
faq.a: Fish, dairy, eggs, and iodised salt are the main sources; locally, cassava and millet are low in iodine.

faq.q: Why is urinary iodine the best screening test?
faq.a: It reflects recent intake and is inexpensive; spot samples are acceptable in low‑resource settings.

exam: A 3‑year‑old boy from a high‑altitude village has a diffuse goiter and delayed milestones. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Iodine‑deficiency goiter with congenital hypothyroidism; check TSH and free T4.
A pregnant woman in a rural clinic presents with fatigue and cold intolerance. Her TSH is 12 mIU/L. What is the next step? — Start levothyroxine and counsel on iodised salt; monitor TSH in 6 weeks.

A patient with known Hashimoto’s thyroiditis develops sudden hyperthyroidism after starting iodised salt. What explains this? — Iodine loading reverses the Wolff‑Chaikoff effect, precipitating thyrotoxicosis.
You find a patient with a diffuse goiter but normal TSH. What should you do? — Check anti‑TPO antibodies to rule out Hashimoto’s; if negative, consider iodine deficiency and start supplementation.
A neonate has a TSH of 25 mIU/L on screening. What is the most appropriate management? — Refer for confirmatory testing and start levothyroxine promptly to prevent cretinism.

A patient with a history of TB presents with a large goiter and weight loss. What is the differential? — Iodine deficiency, TB thyroiditis, and lymphoma; obtain ultrasound and fine‑needle aspiration if suspicious.
A child with a goiter has a urinary iodine of 80 µg/L. What public health measure is most effective? — Universal salt iodisation; community education on iodised salt use.

A patient with a history of amiodarone therapy develops hypothyroidism. What is the likely mechanism? — Amiodarone contains iodine; it can cause both hypo- and hyperthyroidism by overwhelming the thyroid’s iodine stores.
